### Abstract

This study treats the digital economy as a transformation in the production, measurement, and capture of value under conditions of inexpensive copying and costly discovery. A new architecture does not by itself produce a fairer distribution. As the marginal cost of reproducing information approaches zero, scarcity does not disappear. It migrates toward attention, trust, reputation, computation, data, distribution, and the authority to define access. Platforms coordinate multi-sided markets and lower transaction costs, yet their control of relations, data, and visibility can become durable market power.

The study connects attention markets, information goods and network effects, the “content trap,” the thousand-true-fans hypothesis, and the long tail to the distribution of value. Subscriptions, memberships, collective financing, and direct payments offer different ways to earn income, but do not by themselves give creators ownership of audiences or remove intermediary power. Relationship portability, interface competition, discovery, concentration of control, and the ability to enforce rights must be assessed separately. The technical ability to receive a payment and a creator’s independence are different properties.

**Keywords:** digital economy; attention economy; information goods; network effects; multi-sided platform; creator economy; algorithmic visibility; long tail; direct payments; relationship portability; value distribution.

### Research Question

How do digital networks transform the creation, measurement, and capture of value, and under which institutional conditions do creators or users gain greater control over the economic relationships they help produce?

### Methodology

The study combines information economics, multisided-market theory, research on platform labor, empirical work on recommender systems, cryptoeconomics, and institutional analysis of DAOs. Programmatic texts are tested against peer-reviewed scholarship and materials from the ILO, OECD, UNCTAD, and SEC.

### Chronological Scope

The period 1833–2026 begins with the scaling of advertising-subsidized penny newspapers and extends through information goods, platforms, the creator economy, tokenization, and DAOs. The long arc tracks shifting scarcities rather than a single continuous digital industry.

## Academic Introduction

The phrase “new digital economy” has accompanied successive technological breaks: the commercial internet, platforms, mobile applications, the creator economy, blockchains, and artificial intelligence. Its rhetorical force comes from the suggestion that inherited economic limits have ceased to matter. Information can be copied almost freely; a creator can reach a global audience; a network can scale faster than a firm; a token can supposedly make a user an owner. None of these propositions is a universal law.

Digital goods combine a costly first copy with inexpensive reproduction, but production still requires labor, capital, and infrastructure. Network effects can support dominance, but interact with quality, compatibility, multi-homing, switching costs, and regulation. Direct monetization shortens some chains of intermediation while retaining payments, search, hosting, moderation, and taxation. A token may confer access, a vote, a medium of payment, or a financial claim; token possession does not guarantee profit participation, equal governance, or intellectual-property rights.

The research question is: **how do digital networks transform the creation and capture of value, and under which institutional conditions does a creator or user obtain greater control over the economic relations they help produce?**

The method combines information economics, multi-sided-market theory, research on platform labor, empirical work on recommender systems, cryptoeconomics, and the institutional analysis of DAOs. Programmatic texts by Kevin Kelly, Chris Anderson, Li Jin and Shermin Voshmgir are treated as conceptual projects and primary sources of technological imagination. Their predictions are tested against peer-reviewed work and materials from the ILO, OECD, UNCTAD, and SEC. The analysis separates three questions: where utility arises, who receives income, and who may change the rules. The answers often identify different actors.

In 1833, Benjamin Day’s New York *Sun* sold for one cent and expanded the urban mass readership of newspapers. Tim Wu uses the penny press as an early turn in attention-subsidized media: a low price enlarges circulation, while advertisers purchase access to the audience [2]. It would be inaccurate to call this the first sale of attention in history; advertising and information subsidies predated it. Its significance lies in scaling the relationship among inexpensive content, mass distribution, and advertising finance.

Herbert Simon supplied the general formulation: an abundance of information creates a scarcity of what information consumes—the recipient’s attention [1]. Attention is bounded by time and cognition. It is not literally transferred to advertisers as a commodity. A media service sells a probability of contact, a measurable audience, and an opportunity to affect behavior. Advertising media are therefore multi-sided markets that connect users, advertisers, and content producers while selecting prices and rules for each side [3]. A zero monetary price does not imply an absence of exchange, but neither does it prove that the user is “the product” in every respect. Users receive a service while supplying attention, data, and behavioral signals.

Digital platforms increased the precision and speed of this model. A search query signals intent; a feed records reaction; an advertising auction matches advertisers and users in real time. Data reduce uncertainty in targeting and make feedback measurable. Commercial value arises less from one click than from the statistical capacity to predict relevance across many cases.

It does not follow that all digital advertising sells secret psychological profiles or that every algorithm maximizes only time spent. Platforms optimize multiple and changing objectives, including predicted engagement, quality, safety, retention, and commercial outcomes. The scientific task is to establish which metrics are rewarded and which costs remain external to the operator, not to assign one hidden intention to a heterogeneous system.

The attention economy nevertheless produces a structural asymmetry. A platform observes many participants and can run experiments; an individual sees only a personal interface. Advertisers pay for measurable access while users rarely know the marginal commercial significance of their signals. This asymmetry supports transparency, data-protection, and anti-manipulation rules. It cannot be solved simply by paying each person for every datum, because the value of an aggregate prediction is not the sum of independent “prices” of individual records.

Wu’s history thus reveals the institutionalization of scarcity rather than the theft of a fixed substance. When information becomes abundant, the ordering of visibility becomes an asset. The next issue is why the owner of that order can hold power so persistently.
